claimBoundary: A curated set of established reactions, not a ranking of memes trending today. Dated articles and public template archives support usage. Recent Instagram/X evidence below concerns named examples or the wider Brahmanandam meme culture; it does not establish that every variant is currently popular on both platforms.
visualChecks: All 24 final files inspected at 320px, desktop176px and phone240px widths.
Two revised crops made Baburao and Padmanabha Simha clearer.
Spider-Man retains both figures; Two Buttons retains both comic panels; This Is Fine retains the first two panels; Majnu retains the whole painting.
Original low-resolution texture retained for Surprised Pikachu, Michael Scott, Khan Dada and some circulated video frames. No upscaling model or generative reconstruction used.

popularityEvidence.supports: Reports Anil Kapoor sharing a fan-made AI fashion recreation using Majnu’s painting. Supports continued reuse of the painting meme; the acquired asset is the original film prop, not that AI image.
popularityEvidence.verification: Public article text reviewed; direct X post not independently opened.

popularityEvidence.supports: Interview describes Goutham sending film-expression memes to Brahmanandam and their continuing use as stickers/reactions. Wider culture evidence, not a popularity measure for each of these six variants.
Reports Brahmanandam thanking meme creators for keeping his film expressions relevant to younger audiences.
popularityEvidence.verification: Search-indexed full article text read; direct open returned403.

popularityEvidence.supports: Reports Akshay Kumar reusing the familiar twenty-five-day line in an Instagram caption. Historical reuse, not a current trend claim.
Reports Uber India reusing the no-risk phrase in a New Year caption. Used only as reuse evidence; its film attribution is not the primary scene source.
Reports a gathering of meme creators and embeds a public Instagram post. Historical culture evidence; not treated as a license or permission receipt.

entries.name: This Is Fine
entries.sourceContext: K.C. Green’s Question Hound calmly drinks in a burning room. The familiar two-panel reaction is ironic reassurance amid visible trouble: it can acknowledge overwhelm or denial, rather than praise ignoring a problem.
entries.credit: K.C. Green — Gunshow #648, On Fire (2013), first two panels; template via Imgflip.

entries.name: Two Buttons
entries.sourceContext: Jake Clark’s comic pairs two competing buttons with a sweating decision-maker. The template expresses conflicting impulses or an awkward choice; the buttons have no universal meaning until a situation supplies one.
entries.credit: Jake Clark — Daily Struggle comic (2014); blank-label template via Imgflip.

entries.name: Confused Travolta
entries.sourceContext: Vincent Vega looks around Mia Wallace’s room while hearing her over an intercom. The reaction conveys confusion, missing context or looking for something that should be there; it concerns the character’s moment, not John Travolta’s personality.
entries.credit: Miramax / A Band Apart — John Travolta as Vincent Vega in Pulp Fiction (1994); still via Know Your Meme.

entries.name: Pointing Rick Dalton
entries.source: Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019)
entries.sourceContext: Rick Dalton points at the television when he recognizes his own appearance. The reaction is excited recognition of a familiar detail or connection, not proof that every perceived pattern is meaningful.
entries.credit: Columbia Pictures — Leonardo DiCaprio as Rick Dalton in Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019); still via Know Your Meme.

entries.name: Gatsby’s Toast
entries.sourceContext: Jay Gatsby raises a glass during his introduction. The reaction commonly offers congratulations, praise or friendly agreement; it does not turn Gatsby’s broader story into a promise of wealth or success.
entries.credit: Warner Bros. Pictures / Village Roadshow Pictures — Leonardo DiCaprio as Jay Gatsby in The Great Gatsby (2013); still via Know Your Meme.

entries.name: Spider-Man Pointing
entries.sourceContext: Spider-Man and an impersonator point at each other in Double Identity. The two-figure meme highlights a comical resemblance or mutual recognition; preserve both figures rather than treating this as a single Spider-Man portrait.
entries.credit: Marvel / Grantray-Lawrence Animation — Spider-Man, Double Identity (1967); two-character still via Know Your Meme.

entries.name: One Does Not Simply
entries.source: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (2001)
entries.sourceContext: At the Council of Elrond, Boromir explains why entering Mordor is difficult. The meme pushes back on an oversimplified plan: acknowledge the real steps and obstacles without declaring the task impossible.
entries.credit: New Line Cinema — Sean Bean as Boromir in The Fellowship of the Ring (2001); captioned still via Know Your Meme.

entries.name: Picard Facepalm
entries.source: Star Trek: The Next Generation — Déjà Q (1990)
entries.sourceContext: Jean-Luc Picard places his hand over his face in Déjà Q. The familiar reaction expresses exasperation, embarrassment or recognition of an avoidable mistake; use self-aware humour without calling the reader foolish.
entries.credit: Paramount Television — Patrick Stewart as Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation, Déjà Q (1990); still via Know Your Meme.

entries.name: Surprised Pikachu
entries.source: Pokémon: Bulbasaur and the Hidden Village (1997)
entries.sourceContext: Pikachu’s open-mouthed expression comes from Bulbasaur and the Hidden Village. Online it often follows a foreseeable consequence that still surprises someone; the joke is the gap between expectation and outcome, not a prediction of future harm.
entries.credit: Pokémon / OLM — Pikachu anime reaction, Bulbasaur and the Hidden Village (1997); canonical low-resolution meme crop via Know Your Meme.

entries.name: Is This a Pigeon?
entries.source: The Brave Fighter of Sun Fighbird (1991)
entries.sourceContext: The android Yutaro Katori mistakes a butterfly for a pigeon while learning about Earth. The meme playfully examines mislabelling or mistaken assumptions; it is a prompt to check understanding, not an insult to curiosity.
entries.credit: Sunrise / Nagoya TV — The Brave Fighter of Sun Fighbird (1991), Yutaro Katori and butterfly; still via Know Your Meme.

entries.name: I Understood That Reference
entries.sourceContext: Steve Rogers recognizes Nick Fury’s reference to The Wizard of Oz. The reaction celebrates catching a shared reference or finding common ground, rather than suggesting expertise in an unrelated subject.
entries.credit: Marvel Studios — Chris Evans as Steve Rogers in The Avengers (2012); captioned still via Know Your Meme.

entries.name: Michael Scott’s “No!”
entries.sourceContext: Michael Scott reacts dramatically to Toby’s return in Frame Toby. The reaction exaggerates reluctance toward an unwanted development; use it for ordinary comic frustration, not to mock a person’s pain or worth.
entries.credit: NBC / Universal Television — Steve Carell as Michael Scott in The Office, Frame Toby (2008); still via Know Your Meme.

entries.name: Control, Uday
entries.sourceContext: Uday Shetty tells himself to stay in control when frustrated. The reaction is a humorous pause before responding impulsively, and concerns the fictional scene rather than Nana Patekar’s private character.
entries.credit: Welcome (2007), produced by Firoz A. Nadiadwala — Nana Patekar as Uday Shetty; still via Indian Meme Templates.

entries.name: Majnu Bhai’s Painting
entries.sourceContext: Majnu Bhai’s painting places a donkey on a horse. Its improbable composition became a playful reference for unconventional creations and surprising combinations; the joke should not demean someone learning to make art.
entries.credit: Welcome (2007), produced by Firoz A. Nadiadwala — painting prop associated with Anil Kapoor’s Majnu Bhai; template via Imgflip.

entries.name: Raju’s 25-Day Promise
entries.sourceContext: Raju repeats a promise that money will double in twenty-five days. The scheme fails in the film, so the meme is useful for inflated promises and wishful shortcuts, never as financial advice or a forecast of prosperity.
entries.credit: Phir Hera Pheri (2006), produced by Firoz A. Nadiadwala — Akshay Kumar as Raju; captioned still via Humornama.

entries.name: Raju’s Revealed Scheme
entries.source: Phir Hera Pheri (2006): Raju and Pappu
entries.sourceContext: Raju complains that Pappu is saying the scheme aloud. The familiar reaction comments on giving away a plan too soon or an accidental spoiler; it does not endorse secrecy that harms someone.
entries.credit: Phir Hera Pheri (2006) — Akshay Kumar as Raju and Rajpal Yadav as Pappu; source clip via Tenor, uploader attribution retained.

entries.name: Kehna Kya Chahte Ho?
entries.sourceContext: The machine-class professor asks Rancho to say plainly what he means. This reaction requests clarity when an explanation becomes needlessly complicated. The professor is played by Achyut Potdar, not Boman Irani or Akhil Mishra.
entries.credit: Vinod Chopra Films — Achyut Potdar as the machine-class professor in 3 Idiots (2009); captioned still via Humornama.

entries.name: Baburao Takes No Risks
entries.sourceContext: Baburao’s emphatic no-risk reaction became a comic shorthand for checking carefully or refusing an unnecessary gamble. It can expose overcaution as well as prudence; the scene is not a guarantee that any choice is safe.
entries.credit: Hera Pheri (2000), produced by A. G. Nadiadwala — Paresh Rawal as Baburao; scene template via Imgflip.

entries.name: Bhattu Spots the Double Act
entries.sourceContext: Bhattu reacts to another person’s double act in Adhurs. The scene template conveys comic suspicion about inconsistent behaviour; connect it to observable mixed signals, not a claim to know another person’s hidden motives.
entries.credit: Adhurs (2010), Sri Sai Ganesh Productions — Brahmanandam as Bhattu; scene template via Lyricalwoods.

entries.name: Padmanabha Simha’s Brave Talk
entries.sourceContext: Padmanabha Simha declares that there is no need to fear anyone. The comic scene can mirror putting on a brave face before a challenge; it does not establish that the real situation has no risks.
entries.credit: Baadshah (2013), Parameswara Art Productions — Brahmanandam as Padmanabha Simha; first scene panel via Lyricalwoods.

entries.name: Kill Bill Pandey Arrives
entries.source: Race Gurram (2014): Inspector Kill Bill Pandey
entries.sourceContext: Inspector Kill Bill Pandey’s exaggerated entrance became a celebrated comic highlight of Race Gurram. The reaction signals theatrical confidence or calling in an unexpectedly forceful helper; use the comic energy without glorifying violence.
entries.credit: Race Gurram (2014), Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Productions — Brahmanandam as Inspector Kill Bill Pandey; clip via Telugu FilmNagar/Tenor.

entries.name: Padmasri’s Confident Nod
entries.sourceContext: Padmasri’s nod is circulated as a yes-or-agreement reaction. He is the aspiring performer in Dookudu, not Baadshah’s Padmanabha Simha; this specific meme conveys confident assent rather than general wisdom.
entries.credit: 14 Reels Entertainment — Brahmanandam as Padmasri in Dookudu (2011); reaction clip via Tenor.

entries.name: Chary Wants to Stay Out
entries.sourceContext: Chary asks not to be involved. The established reaction expresses reluctance to join someone else’s dispute or extra drama; it can support a boundary without assuming that avoidance is always the right choice.
entries.credit: Dhee (2007), produced by Mallidi Satyanarayana Reddy — Brahmanandam as Chary with Vishnu Manchu; source clip via Kulfy/Tenor.

entries.name: Khan Dada’s Swagger
entries.sourceContext: Khan Dada takes his imagined star power very seriously in Money. The scene reaction playfully contrasts self-image with reality: enjoy a burst of confidence while checking whether preparation supports it.
entries.credit: Money (1993), produced by Ram Gopal Varma — Brahmanandam as Khan Dada; scene image via Chai Bisket.
